extracted.intended_audience: IPO members, patent practitioners, policymakers, legislators, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: A proposed legislative amendment to 35 U.S.C. § 101 and accompanying explanatory guidance defining what subject matter is patent eligible and prescribing how eligibility should be assessed (e.g., claim-as-a-whole, excluding §§102/103/112 considerations). Intended to restore broad, technology-neutral eligibility consistent with the 1952 Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: 101(a) Eligible Subject Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed statutory text: "Whoever invents or discovers, and claims as an invention, any useful process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or any useful improvement thereto, shall be entitled to a patent for a claimed invention thereof, subject only to the exceptions, conditions, and requirements set forth in this Title."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses the broad, technology-neutral categories of patentable subject matter intended by Congress in the 1952 Act; frames eligibility as categorical (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or useful improvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: 101(b) Sole Exception to Subject Matter Eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed statutory text: "A claimed invention is ineligible under subsection (a) if and only if the claimed invention as a whole, as understood by a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains, exists in nature independently of and prior to any human activity, or exists solely in the human mind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the only two categorical exceptions to eligibility: (1) things that exist in nature independently of human activity (laws of nature, natural products) and (2) things that exist solely in the human mind (purely mental phenomena/abstract ideas). Emphasizes assessment of the claimed invention as a whole and as understood by POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: 101(c) Sole Eligibility Standard — exclusion of §§102, 103, and 112 and inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed statutory text: "The eligibility of a claimed invention under subsections (a) and (b) shall be determined without regard as to the requirements or conditions of sections 102, 103, and 112 of this Title, the manner in which the claimed invention was made or discovered, or the claimed invention's inventive concept."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressly prohibits importing novelty, nonobviousness, written description/enablement, manner of making, or the 'inventive concept' inquiry into the §101 eligibility analysis. Intended to preserve the separation between categorical eligibility (§101) and patentability/merits ( §§102/103/112 ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate eligibility for the claimed invention 'as a whole' (no point-of-novelty dissection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance repeatedly emphasizes that eligibility must be assessed for the invention "as a whole" and not by dissecting claims into old and new elements or isolating a 'point of novelty' (cites Diehr and critical discussion of Flook/Benson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disapproves of claim dissection into old/new elements to determine eligibility; rejects the 'point-of-novelty' approach and directs courts/examiners to consider the entire claimed invention in context rather than isolating individual limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude novelty/nonobviousness/enablement considerations from §101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated explanation that the §101 inquiry should not consider the conditions or requirements of §§102, 103, or 112 (novelty, non-obviousness, written description/enablement), nor be influenced by whether elements are 'conventional, routine, well understood.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses and rejects the practice (in Mayo/Alice line) of treating lack of novelty or conventionality as evidence that a claim is merely 'something more' or not 'significantly more.' Such determinations belong to §§102/103/112; using them in §101 conflates distinct statutory functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligibility if the claimed invention 'exists in nature independently of and prior to any human activity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive guidance: this ineligibility criterion targets laws of nature and natural products — anything that existed in nature independently of human activity is not eligible. The requirement of 'independently of any human activity' captures the idea that inventions must be the result of some human act upon nature (i.e., 'made by man').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the distinction with Myriad (cDNA vs genomic DNA): cDNA did not exist in nature independently of human activity and therefore could be patent eligible; notes ambiguity around 'isolated' gDNA and explains why 'activity' was chosen over alternative phrasing (effort, agency, contribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ineligibility if the claimed invention 'exists solely in the human mind' (abstract ideas / mental processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive guidance: this ineligibility criterion is directed to abstract ideas and purely mental phenomena — ideas that do not have physical or tangible aspects (e.g., purely mental processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Returns the abstract idea exception to its original focus on purely mental phenomena (per Benson/Diehr) and states that claim limitations requiring some external involvement with the physical world or a representation thereof (e.g., data in a computer) should be considered eligible. Cites policy reasons (proof problems, First Amendment) for excluding purely mental phenomena from protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit use of 'inventive concept' and 'point-of-novelty' in §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of Mayo/Alice/Flook: the Court's introduction of 'inventive concept' and dissection to find a 'point of novelty' improperly imports §103-type inventiveness into §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed legislation seeks to eliminate 'inventive concept' and 'point-of-novelty' inquiries from the §101 analysis and move such considerations back to §§102/103 where objective novelty/nonobviousness are assessed. Examples discussed include courts treating automation of manual processes as lacking inventive concept (an issue for §103).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA) in eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed statute and notes specify that eligibility is assessed 'as understood by a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains' (POSITA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that applying a POSITA standard makes §101 analysis objective, technology-neutral, and consistent with other patent doctrines (enablement, obviousness, claim construction). A limitation that appears 'abstract' to a court may have technical meaning to POSITA; POSITA evolves with technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-neutral, broad construction consistent with the 1952 Act ('anything under the sun made by man')
rubrics_metrics.description: Background and legislative history emphasize that Congress intended §101 to be construed broadly — 'anything under the sun that is made by man' — and that the 1952 Act removed subjective 'invention' inquiries from §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports restoring broad, technology-neutral eligibility and recognizes processes that are new uses of known processes (section 100(b)). The proposal frames the amendment as returning to congressional intent and preventing judicial narrowing over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat use of generic computers or conventional components alone as rendering claims ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: The notes criticize the prevalent practice of invalidating claims because they merely use 'generic hardware and software' or conventional computer implementation, which courts have used post-Alice to find ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed amendment and commentary argue that applying existing technology (e.g., generic computers) for new purposes should not be a §101 disqualification; whether a claim is merely an automation of conventional practice is a merits question more properly addressed under §§102/103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid subjective, unpredictable §101 tests; seek predictability and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The commentary repeatedly notes that the current §101 jurisprudence (Mayo/Alice) is subjective, unpredictable, and provides limited practical guidance, undermining incentives to innovate and consistent examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal aims to simplify the eligibility analysis, restore objective standards (e.g., POSITA viewpoint and categorical exclusions narrowly defined), and promote predictable, consistent outcomes for examiners, courts, applicants, and the public.
